drills.coachNote: White's plan is simple: keep those connected pawns on d6 and e6 rolling forward while Rb6 checks your king out of position first. Kd8 walks straight into that — Rb8+ forces Nc8, jamming your own rook on h8, and after c6 White's pieces coordinate to overrun your position, flipping your -2.7 edge into a loss. Kc8 sidesteps the check entirely; the fight still gets sharp after c6 Bc4 dxe7 Kc7 Rb7+, but your rook and bishop stay coordinated instead of your whole queenside caving in. drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here — bishop up with connected pawns on both wings — and Black's king can only shuffle around hoping you misplace something. Kf4 isn't a disaster, but it's not the cleanest: it lets Black's king pick up a free tempo with Kf7 while your own king wanders instead of directly supporting your pawn breaks. Kf3 does the same job more efficiently, tucking in behind the e3 pawn ready to push e4 without giving Black anything to work with, and the game still marches forward the same way — Kf7, e4, Ke7, Ke3. In endings this lopsided the result never changes, but every king move should still have a job.

Ba2 gets there directly, and your king marches straight in behind it — Kc4, then Kb5, heading for b6 and c7 while Black's king can only watch. drills.coachNote: Black has a mating net forming around your king on e1 — the rook on f2 controls the second rank, the queen on g5 can swing in, and your knight on d2 is the only thing standing in the way. drills.coachNote: White's real plan is simple: push the a6/b6 pawn duo home with the rook on e6 shepherding them. Rc4+ feels natural, but a check is only good if it hurts your opponent — this one just kicks the king to d5, exactly the square it wants, helping support the pawn's push to b7, and you then had to spend a move getting your rook behind it with Rb3, letting nearly four pawns of your winning margin slip away. Rc1 was the sturdier idea: get behind the pawns first, and only check when it actually pushes White's king somewhere worse — after b7, Re1+ shoves the king away from d5, and Rb1 stops the pawn cold. Save your checks for when they work against your opponent's plan, not with it.

drills.coachNote: White's a6 and b5 pawns are connected and dangerously advanced, and the only real way to stop passers like that is to plant your rook on one of their files before they roll. Rc7 sits on neither file, so it changes nothing — White pushes b6 then b7, and by the time your rook arrives via ...Rc1-Ra1 it's watching the a-file while the pawn about to queen is on b8, and a completely winning position is gone. Ra7 fixes it at once, freezing the a-pawn in front of your rook so your king is free to march over with ...Kh5-Kd6. Against connected passers, get your rook onto one of their files right away.

drills.coachNote: Black is almost out of resources here — with every pawn frozen, the bishop's g4-h3 shuffle and a few king moves are all that's keeping the position alive, and your job is to squeeze those away before advancing. Kc6 doesn't do that: after ...Bg4, Kd6, ...Kf8, Re7 the bishop keeps the better square g4 instead of being pushed to h3, which is why the evaluation dropped so sharply even though you're still clearly better. Kb4 is the patient version — it lets ...Bh3, Kc5, ...Kd8, Kd6, ...Kc8 follow, shoving the bishop to its worst square and the king back to c8 before your king has to do the work. In locked positions like this, force the opponent's mobile piece to its worst square before you advance.
